Its earlier origin is unknown; one view holds that it may have been brought in by Swedes during the Thirty Years' War, another that it descends from the medieval psaltery. The Val-d'Ajol type is recorded in 1730 and went from four strings to five, its diatonic frets rising from 14 to 17 during the nineteenth century. The Gérardmer type is recorded in 1723, was built by makers or players themselves, later fell out of favour, and was revived after 1945. Instruments of the same kind were once spread across Europe and are now found mainly in Norway, Iceland, Flanders, Hungary and France; the Appalachian dulcimer is a parallel instrument of the rural mountain South of the United States.
沃日山區撥弦琴為齊特琴族撥弦樂器，以指、鵝羽或撥片掃弦，也可指彈、小棒擊弦或弓拉: The épinette des Vosges is a plucked instrument of the zither family, strummed with the fingers, a goose quill or a plectrum, and also played fingerstyle, struck with small sticks or bowed. Its range is about two and a half octaves and it can produce a seven-note scale; the Val-d'Ajol type is tuned to open C major and has additional chromatic frets for changing key. When the left hand stops the strings with a smooth wooden stick it produces a sliding metallic sound and a marked portamento. Unlike other dulcimer-type instruments, the melody strings and the drone strings are separate and can be struck separately to set up a rhythm; the volume can be adjusted by strumming all the strings, only the melody strings, or the two groups separately.

The épinette des Vosges is a traditional plucked instrument of the zither family from the Val-d'Ajol and Gérardmer area of the Vosges mountains in France, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122. The body is fretted and the number of strings varies with the type, commonly three to eight; the small ones are about fifty to sixty centimetres long and the large ones about eighty. Players mostly sit, resting the instrument on a table or on the knee, stopping the frets with the left hand and plucking with the thumb, a goose quill or a plectrum; it can also be played fingerstyle, struck or bowed. It is made and played by local musicians or instrument makers, and its use has long been confined to those two places.
演奏者通常坐姿，將琴置於桌上，或放於腿上並向外傾斜。調音憑耳調，可依伴奏樂器、琴: Players usually sit, with the instrument on a table, or on the lap tilted outwards. It is tuned by ear, and may be tuned higher or lower to suit an accompanying instrument, the pitch of the instrument or personal preference. The right hand may sweep the thumb, a goose quill or a plectrum across all the melody and drone strings, or pluck only the melody strings; there is also fingerstyle playing, striking with small sticks and bowing. The left hand may stop the strings with the fingers, or slide a smooth wooden or reed stick along them to produce a portamento. A beginner can start with the diatonic scale and telling the melody strings from the drone strings, then gradually add strumming, striking and sliding.
